title: Quiet Hours

coach.board: Tabs switch between your rules, the charts, tonight's timeline and the Alertmanager route. Every rule decides who gets woken, and the page count is what you are keeping low.
coach.actions: Next hour moves time on one step and Run to morning plays the rest. Rules cost a move to change; time is free.
coach.firstMove: Read each warm-up graph and pick what to do with it, then open the Rules tab and read what a rule fires on.

lossRule: The Sleep or SLO score fell: you were paged for noise, or a real incident went unnoticed.

events.title: Error ratio jumps to 8% for 20 minutes
events.fix: Users feel the error ratio, so alert on it: errors divided by all requests, with `for: 5m`. A ratio holds at any traffic level; an absolute error count does not.

events.title: A harmless traffic surge for twelve minutes
events.fix: More traffic means more errors in absolute terms and a hotter CPU, but users are fine. A ratio ignores the surge; a count or a CPU threshold pages for nothing.

events.title: A one-minute CPU blip
events.fix: One bad evaluation is noise. `for:` makes the condition hold across evaluations before the alert fires, and a cause such as CPU belongs at `warning` unless users are hurt.

events.title: p95 latency creeps up for two hours
events.fix: A small share of slow requests moves the tail a lot and the mean only a little. Read a histogram with `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` over the `_bucket` series; an average hides it.

events.title: The data disk starts filling at 12% an hour
events.fix: A static threshold (alert at 5% free) fires with minutes to spare. `predict_linear` projects the trend and fires hours before the disk is full, while there is still time to act.

events.title: All 15 targets miss one scrape, then recover
events.fix: A one-minute scrape flap is not an outage. `for: 2m` or longer lets it pass, and `group_by` keeps one alert per rule from becoming fifteen pages.

events.title: A whole rack goes dark: 15 targets down for 25 minutes
events.fix: One real incident raises fifteen alerts. Alertmanager's `group_by: [alertname, job]` turns them into a single notification instead of fifteen pages.

events.title: The request-rate panel takes ten seconds to load
events.fix: An expensive query recomputed on every refresh is slow. A recording rule precomputes it under a `level:metric:operations` name, and the panel queries the cheap series.

levels.title: 1. First shift
levels.blurb: Classify four signals, then fix two starter rules that are too twitchy. Page me for the real error spike, and let me sleep through traffic surges and a CPU blip. Rules are free to change all night, but the pages you earn are not.
hints: Do the warm-up first: read each graph, then choose its type and what to do with it before you alert.
A counter only goes up, so alert on its rate. The twitchy rules fire on blips and surges you should sleep through.
Make the error rule use the error ratio over several minutes with a for duration, make CPU a warning, then Run to morning.
path: Classify signal 1: a counter, alert with rate
Classify signal 2: a gauge, alert with nothing
Classify signal 3: a histogram, alert with histogram_quantile
Classify signal 4: a summary, alert with nothing
lessons: A counter only goes up, so alert on its rate; classify a signal (counter, gauge, histogram, summary) before you write a rule.
Add a for duration so a blip does not page you, and send non-urgent alerts as warnings that wait for the morning.

tryItForReal.commands:
groups:
  - name: starter
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRatio
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) > 0.05
        for: 5m
        labels: { severity: critical }

promtool check rules rules.yml

warmup.hint: Every request served. It only ever goes up, and drops to 0 when the process restarts.
warmup.why: http_requests_total only goes up, so it is a counter: graph rate() of it, never the raw line.

warmup.hint: Jobs waiting right now. It goes up and down.
warmup.why: job_queue_depth goes up and down, so it is a gauge: it already means something, so graph it as it is.

warmup.hint: Counts of requests that finished within each latency bucket, plus _sum and _count.
warmup.why: Buckets plus _sum and _count make a histogram: histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) turns them into a percentile.

warmup.hint: A latency percentile the client library already computed, one value per instance.
warmup.why: Pre-computed quantiles are a summary. Read them as they are: they cannot be averaged across instances.

levels.title: 2. Slow burn
levels.blurb: Two quiet killers: p95 latency creeping up over two hours, and a disk that fills in the small hours. Averages and static thresholds notice too late. Alert on the tail and on where the disk is heading.

warmup.hint: Latency as counts per bucket. The average hides the slow tail; the tail is where users hurt.
warmup.why: Buckets plus _sum and _count make a histogram: histogram_quantile(0.95, ...) shows the slow tail that an average hides.

warmup.hint: Free space on the disk. It slides down through the night and nobody clears it.
warmup.why: A gauge that is running out: predict_linear() says when it will reach zero, hours before it does, which is when you want the page.

hints: Do the warm-up first: read the latency and disk graphs and choose what to do with each before you alert.
An average and a fixed threshold notice too late. Alert on the tail (p95 with histogram_quantile) and on where the disk is heading (predict_linear), not where it is now.
Save a p95 latency rule and a DiskFillingUp rule using predict_linear, keep CPU as a warning, then Run to morning.
path: Classify signal 1: a histogram, alert with histogram_quantile
Classify signal 2: a gauge, alert with predict_linear
lessons: Alert on the tail (histogram_quantile) and not the average, which hides the slow requests.
Alert on where a resource is heading with predict_linear, not on where it is right now.

tryItForReal.commands:
- alert: HighP95Latency
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))) > 0.5
  for: 5m
- alert: DiskFillingUp
  expr: predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes[1h], 4 * 3600) < 0
  for: 5m

levels.title: 3. Storm night
levels.blurb: The earlier rules are in place. Now a rack goes dark and fifteen alerts fire at once, a scrape flap looks like an outage, and the request-rate panel is too slow to use while you debug. Group the storm, tame the flap, and record the expensive query.

warmup.hint: 1 while a target answers its scrape, 0 when it does not. A scrape that times out for a minute flips it to 0 and back.
warmup.why: up is a gauge of 1 or 0 per target: alert on it as it is, with a for: clause so one missed scrape does not page you.

hints: Read the up graph in the warm-up, then look at the Route tab: with nothing grouped, fifteen alerts mean fifteen pages.
Group by alertname and job so a dead rack is one page, ride out a flapping scrape with a for clause, and record the expensive query as a rule.
Set group_by to alertname,job, save the InstanceDown rule with a for duration, add a recording rule for the request rate, then Run to morning.
path: Classify signal 1: a gauge, alert with nothing
lessons: Group alerts by what they share (group_by: [alertname, job]) so a dead rack is one page, not fifteen.
Use a for clause to ride out a flapping scrape, and record an expensive query as a recording rule so dashboards stay fast.

tryItForReal.commands:
# alertmanager.yml
route:
  group_by: [alertname, job]
  group_wait: 30s

# rules.yml
- record: job:http_requests:rate5m
  expr: sum by (job) (rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
- alert: InstanceDown
  expr: up == 0
  for: 2m
